batchName: Late Republic: The Social War and Sulla (91-78 BCE) - Easy Batch 2
chapterName: Late Republic: The Social War and Sulla (91-78 BCE)

questions.question: What did the Julian Law (lex Iulia) of October 90 BC offer to Italian communities?
options: Return of all public land seized from them since 133 BC
Citizenship for those that stayed loyal or quickly laid down arms
Permanent exemption from sending soldiers to Rome's wars
A fixed share of plunder from the coming wars in the East
questions.explanation: The Julian Law granted Roman citizenship to loyal communities and those that surrendered quickly. A second law in 89 BC extended the offer to almost everyone, and support for the rebellion drained away.
questions.sourceQuote: It let any Italian community that had stayed loyal, or quickly laid down its arms, take up Roman citizenship.

questions.question: What unprecedented step did Sulla take in 88 BC after a new law stripped him of his command?
options: He resigned and went into voluntary exile
He fled to Africa to raise new troops
He defected to the side of Mithridates
He led his army on Rome itself
questions.explanation: Sulla went to his army near Nola and marched it on Rome, something no Roman general had ever done. He took the city and had Marius declared a public enemy.
questions.sourceQuote: He went to his army near Nola, warned the soldiers they would lose the plunder of the East, and led them on Rome.

questions.question: Who wrote the fullest surviving narrative of the Social War?
options: A Greek historian writing more than two centuries later
A Roman senator writing in the year after the war
A Samnite officer who fought at the siege of Asculum
Sulla himself, in the memoirs he wrote in retirement
questions.explanation: The main account comes from a Greek historian writing nearly two hundred years after the events. Most ancient writers agreed with his citizenship-centred story.
questions.sourceQuote: The fullest surviving narrative was written by a Greek historian more than two centuries later.

questions.question: In which town did the killing of a Roman magistrate and every Roman resident set off the allied revolt?
options: Corfinium
Nola
Bovianum
Asculum
questions.explanation: A Roman magistrate heard that Asculum, in Picenum, was swapping hostages and rushed there to threaten the townspeople. Terrified of discovery, they killed him and every Roman in the town.
questions.sourceQuote: Late in 91 or early in 90 BC, a Roman magistrate heard that Asculum, a town in Picenum near Italy's Adriatic coast, was swapping hostages.

questions.question: Which veteran general turned the tide in 90 BC after seeing bodies floating downstream and forcing the river crossing?
options: Sulla
Drusus
Cinna
Marius
questions.explanation: Marius, who had earlier saved Italy from Germanic invaders, forced the river and won. With Sulla's help he beat the Marsi again and split the rebels into northern and southern halves.
questions.sourceQuote: Marius, the veteran general who had saved Italy from Germanic invaders, saw bodies floating downstream, forced the river and won.

questions.question: What was unusual about Sulla's family background?
options: He came from a rich merchant family in Asia Minor
He was the son of a freed slave from Campania
His ancient noble family had sunk into poverty
His family were Samnites who had won citizenship
questions.explanation: Sulla was born in 138 BC into one of Rome's oldest noble families, but it had little money. He spent his youth among actors, musicians and dancers.
questions.sourceQuote: Sulla was born in 138 BC into one of Rome's oldest noble families, but a family that had sunk into poverty.

questions.question: How did the young Sulla win fame during the war in Numidia?
options: By negotiating a lasting peace treaty with the king
By persuading a neighbouring ruler to betray the rebel king
By killing the rebel king in single combat on the field
By storming the Numidian capital with a small force
questions.explanation: Sulla got a neighbouring ruler to hand the rebellious king over to Rome. Marius took the credit, and their friendship soured into rivalry.
questions.sourceQuote: Sulla won fame by persuading a neighbouring ruler to betray the king into Roman hands.

questions.question: What did Sulla do after laying down the dictatorship around the start of 80 BC?
options: Had himself crowned king before the assembled Senate
Walked unguarded through the Forum, offering to answer any citizen
Set out at once on a new campaign against Parthia
Named his chief officer as dictator in his place
questions.explanation: Sulla dismissed his guards and walked unprotected through the Forum. He then held a final consulship in 80 BC before retiring.
questions.sourceQuote: He dismissed his guards and walked unprotected through the Forum, offering to answer any citizen.

questions.question: What did Rome's Italian allies (socii) have to provide in return for keeping their land and running their own affairs?
options: Soldiers whenever Rome went to war
An annual tribute paid in silver
Grain shipments for the city of Rome
Hostages from their leading families
questions.explanation: The allies' treaties obliged them to send troops for Rome's wars. In exchange they shared in the plunder, and Rome often backed local elites against popular uprisings.
questions.sourceQuote: In return, they had to send soldiers whenever Rome went to war.

questions.question: Where did Sulla spend his retirement, writing his memoirs?
options: A villa near Puteoli on the Bay of Naples
A country villa outside Brundisium
A house in Athens among Greek scholars
An estate in the mountains near Corfinium
questions.explanation: Sulla retired to his villa near Puteoli after a final consulship in 80 BC. There he wrote his memoirs and kept company with actors and musicians.
questions.sourceQuote: After a final consulship in 80 BC, Sulla retired to his villa near Puteoli, a port on the Bay of Naples.
